paragraphs.title: Writing the Prophecy of Return and Distress

easy.explanation: Verse 1 says, "The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord."
easy.q: To whom did the word of the Lord come?

answers: Write the words in a book
easy.explanation: The Lord commanded him, "Write thee all the words... in a book."
easy.q: What did the Lord command Jeremiah to do?

easy.explanation: The Lord promised to bring back His people Israel and Judah.
easy.q: Who would be brought back to the land?

answers: The writing records God's promise of return
The writing describes only a war
medium.explanation: Jeremiah was told to record all the words God had spoken, including the promise of restoration.
medium.q: What is the connection between writing the words and the promise about the future?

medium.explanation: The phrase means that God would restore His people from captivity and bring them back.
medium.q: In this passage, what does "bring again the captivity" mean?

medium.explanation: The verse says they would return to the land and "possess it."
medium.q: What would Israel and Judah do after returning to the land?

answers: The prophecy was to be preserved as a written record
The prophecy was meant to be spoken only
The prophecy concerned only the past
challenge.explanation: The command to write the words shows that the prophecy was to be recorded and preserved.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the command to write all these words in a book?

answers: Captivity contrasted with return to the land
A king contrasted with a priest
A city contrasted with a wilderness
challenge.explanation: The passage contrasts captivity with God's promise to return the people to their land.
challenge.q: What major contrast appears at the beginning of the prophecy?

answers: To present the people as both parts together
challenge.explanation: The promise concerns both Israel and Judah, bringing the divided people together.
challenge.q: Why are both Israel and Judah mentioned?

paragraphs.title: The Day of Distress and the Promise of Liberation

answers: A voice of trembling and fear
easy.explanation: Verse 5 says, "We have heard a voice of trembling, of fear, and not of peace."
easy.q: What was heard according to the passage?

easy.explanation: The Lord promised, "I will break his yoke from off thy neck."
easy.q: What would the Lord break from Israel's neck?

easy.explanation: The Lord said, "Fear thou not... neither be dismayed, O Israel."
easy.q: What were Jacob and Israel told not to do?

medium.explanation: The image of labor pains describes the terror and suffering of the people.
medium.q: What does the question about a man travailing with child illustrate?

medium.explanation: In context, "bonds" means restraints or chains that held the people in bondage.
medium.q: What are the "bonds" that the Lord would burst?

answers: All would be saved in the same way
The nations would be ended, but Israel would not be completely ended
Israel would be ended while the nations would be saved
medium.explanation: God would make a full end of the nations, but He would not make a full end of Israel.
medium.q: What is the difference between the judgment on the nations and the judgment on Israel?

answers: As a day unlike any other
challenge.explanation: It is called a great day, "so that none is like it."
challenge.q: How is the day described in verse 7?

answers: Israel would no longer serve strangers
Israel would rule over all nations
challenge.explanation: After the yoke is broken, "strangers shall no more serve themselves of him."
challenge.q: What major change is promised when the yoke is broken?

answers: A return to security and peace
challenge.explanation: These words describe safety, rest, and freedom from fear.
challenge.q: What does the phrase "in rest, and be quiet, and none shall make him afraid" suggest?

easy.explanation: The passage calls Israel's bruise incurable and its wound grievous.
The passage connects the suffering with the multitude of Israel's iniquity and sins.
easy.q: What caused the wound according to the passage?

easy.explanation: The Lord promised, "I will heal thee of thy wounds."
easy.q: What did the Lord promise to do for Israel's wounds?

answers: There was no one to bind up the wound, and no healing medicines
medium.explanation: The passage says there was none to plead the cause and no healing medicines.
medium.q: Why was there no one to plead Israel's cause at the beginning of the passage?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to remedies that could bring healing to the wound.
medium.q: What does "healing medicines" refer to in this passage?

answers: They would be devoured and taken captive
medium.explanation: The passage says Israel's enemies would be devoured, go into captivity, and become a spoil.
medium.q: What would happen to those who devoured and spoiled Israel?

answers: Sin explains the wound, while God's promise offers healing
The passage connects neither sin nor healing
The punishment removes every possibility of healing
challenge.explanation: Israel's sins explain the judgment, but God still promises to restore and heal it.
challenge.q: How are responsibility, punishment, and hope combined in the passage?

answers: Zion was regarded as abandoned and rejected
Zion was described as a place of healing
challenge.explanation: The statement portrays Zion as forsaken and without anyone seeking her.
challenge.q: What does the name "Zion" suggest in the statement, "This is Zion, whom no man seeketh after"?

answers: Wound, sin, judgment on enemies, and healing
challenge.explanation: The passage begins with the wound, explains its cause, describes judgment on the enemies, and ends with healing.
challenge.q: What is the order of developments in the passage?

paragraphs.title: Restoration of the People and Its Leadership

easy.explanation: The Lord promised to bring again Jacob's captivity and have mercy on his dwellingplaces.
easy.q: What would the Lord do to Jacob's tents and dwellingplaces?

easy.explanation: The passage says, "the city shall be builded upon her own heap."
easy.q: What would happen to the city?

answers: Thanksgiving and the voice of those who make merry
easy.explanation: The passage says that thanksgiving and joyful voices would come from them.
easy.q: What would come from the restored people?

answers: They would be multiplied and not become few
medium.explanation: God promised, "I will multiply them, and they shall not be few."
medium.q: What connection is made between the growth of the people and their restoration?

answers: In its own place and upon its former site
medium.explanation: The phrase indicates that the city would be rebuilt on its own former site.
medium.q: What does "upon her own heap" mean?

medium.explanation: The governor would proceed "from the midst of them."
medium.q: Where would the future governor come from?

answers: Restoration includes social life and joy
challenge.explanation: The passage joins rebuilding with multiplication, thanksgiving, and joyful celebration.
challenge.q: What does the movement from rebuilding the city to thanksgiving and celebration show?

answers: Israel's belonging to God would be renewed
Israel would be separated from God
Israel would rule over every nation
challenge.explanation: The words express a renewed covenant relationship between God and His people.
challenge.q: What is the meaning of the renewed relationship in, "ye shall be my people, and I will be your God"?

answers: He would be able to draw near to God
challenge.explanation: The passage says that the governor would be caused to draw near and would approach God.
challenge.q: How is the future leader described in relation to God?

paragraphs.title: The Storm of Judgment and the Latter Days

easy.explanation: The verse says the continuing whirlwind would fall upon "the head of the wicked."
easy.q: Upon whose head would the Lord's whirlwind fall?

answers: The fierce anger of the Lord
easy.explanation: The fierce anger of the Lord would not return until He had performed the intents of His heart.
easy.q: What would not return until the Lord had completed His purpose?

answers: Only the history of foreign kings
easy.explanation: The passage says, "in the latter days ye shall consider it," referring to God's purpose.
easy.q: What would people understand in the latter days?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to the purposes God intends to carry out.
medium.q: What does "the intents of his heart" mean in this passage?

answers: People will consider and understand God's purpose
medium.explanation: The verse says that in the latter days they would consider God's completed purpose.
medium.q: What will happen in the latter days according to the final verse?

medium.explanation: It is described as a whirlwind going forth with fury and continuing.
medium.q: How is the Lord's whirlwind described?

answers: The future will reveal the meaning of God's purpose
The purpose will be canceled in the future
challenge.explanation: The passage connects the completion of God's purpose with understanding it in the latter days.
challenge.q: What is the connection between completing God's purpose and the latter days?

answers: The storm of judgment contrasts with the restored relationship between God and Israel
challenge.explanation: The chapter includes both severe judgment and the ultimate restoration of God's relationship with His people.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between these closing verses and the earlier restoration verses?

answers: Restored fellowship is the final goal of the process
The passage describes separation from God
challenge.explanation: The covenant relationship shows the intended goal of judgment and restoration.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the repeated relationship between God and His people at the end of the chapter?
